What Is “Information”?
Message A:
The Sun will rise tomorrow.
Message B:
A meteor will hit our school tomorrow.

Which message is more surprising?

units.label: slide 6
units.text:
In information theory:
A less probable event carries more information.

something certain → almost no new information 
something unlikely → much more information 

For the robot:
Forward: 50% → not very surprising 
U-turn: 10% → more surprising 

Information theory measures probability, not how important the message is to a human.

units.label: slide 10

From Information to Entropy
A source produces many different symbols.

Each symbol has:
its probability 
its information value 
We want the average information per symbol.

units.label: slide 11
units.text:
How can we think about Entropy?
Entropy tells us how unpredictable a source is on average. 
Entropy measures how much new information we get from each symbol on average. 
Entropy is the average amount of information carried by each symbol. 
Entropy gives a theoretical lower limit on the average number of bits needed per symbol for lossless encoding.

High entropy → less predictable → more information → harder to compress
Low entropy → more predictable → less information → easier to compress

units.label: slide 12

Our simple code is already extremely close to the theoretical limit.

Detecting and Correcting Errors
Hamming Code (7,4):
 4 data bits, 3 parity bits

P1 checks:		1, 3, 5, 7
P2 checks:		2, 3, 6, 7
P4 checks:		4, 5, 6, 7

units.label: slide 19
units.text:
We want to send data:	1011



P1 checks 1,3,5,7
There are two 1s → P1 = 0

Similarly: P2 = 1	&	P4 = 0

So we transmit:		0110011

units.label: slide 20
units.ocr_text:
Imagine we have received: 0110001

Receiver checks parity:

P12 OK

P2 » FAIL

P4 > FAIL

Failed parity positions: 2+4 = 6, therefore: Error at bit 6
Flipbit6back: 0110011

Key idea:
The pattern of failed parity checks identifies the position of the error.

units.label: slide 22
units.text:
From Entropy to Huffman Coding
Last lessons: frequent symbols should have shorter codes.

How do we systematically decide which code each symbol should get?
How can we make the code both efficient and unambiguous?
Can an algorithm build such a code for us?

units.label: slide 23
units.text:
Huffman coding

lossless compression method 
uses symbol frequencies 
frequent symbols receive shorter codes 
rare symbols receive longer codes 
produces a prefix-free code


*A prefix-free code is a code in which no complete codeword is the beginning of another codeword.

units.label: slide 24
units.text:
How to Build a Huffman Code:

List all symbols and their frequencies. 
Find the two least frequent symbols. 
Join them into one node. 
Add their frequencies. 
Repeat until only one node remains. 
Label branches 0 and 1. 
Read each code from the root to the symbol.
